title: Fourier Analysis of Triangular Waves
short_intro: A triangular wave is a periodic, non-sinusoidal waveform with linear ramps between alternating peak values. Its Fourier series representation consists exclusively of fundamental and odd harmonic components whose amplitudes decay inversely with the square of the harmonic number.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of triangular wave, fundamental frequency, peak-to-peak amplitude, and basic understanding of harmonic content.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Complete Fourier series coefficient evaluation using integral calculus, odd harmonic suppression of even terms, power spectrum distribution, and Parseval's relation.

prerequisites: Periodic functions and orthogonality of trigonometric functions
Fourier series expansion for even and odd functions
RMS value and average power of periodic signals

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Waveform Symmetry
bullets: A standard symmetric triangular wave x(t) with period T and peak amplitude A oscillates between -A and +A.
The function possesses odd symmetry about the origin, meaning x(-t) = -x(t), which results in an a_0 average term and all cosine coefficients (a_n) vanishing identically.
The waveform is continuous everywhere, and its first derivative is a square wave with alternating discontinuous steps of finite magnitude.

concept_notes.heading: Harmonic Content and Amplitude Decay
bullets: The Fourier series of a symmetric triangular wave contains only odd harmonics: fundamental, third, fifth, seventh, and so on.
The amplitude of the nth harmonic decreases quadratically as 1/n² relative to the fundamental frequency.
Because of the 1/n² dependence, higher-order harmonics attenuate much faster than those of a square wave (which decay as 1/n), making the triangular wave a smoother waveform.

concept_notes.heading: Power Distribution in Frequency Spectrum
bullets: Total average power of a periodic wave is distributed among its DC and harmonic frequency components.
The RMS value of a triangular wave of peak amplitude A is given by A / sqrt(3).
By Parseval's theorem, the sum of the squares of the RMS values of all harmonic components equals the square of the signal RMS value.

concept_notes.heading: Differentiation and Integration Relations
bullets: The time derivative of a symmetric triangular wave produces a symmetric square wave with the same period.
Conversely, integrating a symmetric square wave yields a triangular wave, highlighting the linear relationship between spectral slopes.
Differentiating a continuous waveform reduces the exponent of its harmonic amplitude decay by 1 (changing 1/n² to 1/n).

derivations.title: Fourier Series of a Symmetric Triangular Wave
derivations.conditions: Symmetric triangular wave defined over [-T/2, T/2] with x(t) = (4A/T)t for 0 <= t <= T/2 and x(t) = -(4A/T)t for -T/2 <= t <= 0
steps: Establish the Fourier series expansion: x(t) = a_0/2 + sum_{n=1}^{infty} [a_n cos(nomega_0 t) + b_n sin(nomega_0 t)] with omega_0 = 2pi/T.
Evaluate a_0 = (2/T) int_{-T/2}^{T/2} x(t) dt = 0 due to odd symmetry, and a_n = (2/T) int_{-T/2}^{T/2} x(t) cos(nomega_0 t) dt = 0 because the integrand is odd.
Calculate the sine coefficients: b_n = (4/T) int_{0}^{T/2} (\frac{4A}{T}t) sin(nomega_0 t) dt.
Integrate by parts: b_n = \frac{16A}{T^2} [ -t \frac{cos(nomega_0 t)}{nomega_0} + \frac{sin(nomega_0 t)}{(nomega_0)^2} ]_{0}^{T/2}.
Substitute limits noting omega_0 T/2 = pi: b_n = \frac{8A}{n^2 pi^2} [ 1 - cos(npi) ].
Simplify for odd n: b_n = \frac{16A}{n^2 pi^2} for n = 1, 3, 5, ... and b_n = 0 for even n.

derivations.title: RMS Value of a Triangular Wave
derivations.conditions: Periodic triangular wave with peak amplitude A and period T
steps: Write the definition of root-mean-square value: X_{rms} = sqrt{ \frac{1}{T} int_{0}^{T} [x(t)]^2 dt }.
Use the linear equation for the first quarter-cycle: x(t) = \frac{4A}{T} t for 0 <= t <= T/4.
Due to symmetry over four identical quarter-cycles, set X_{rms}^2 = \frac{4}{T} int_{0}^{T/4} (\frac{4A}{T} t)^2 dt.
Evaluate the integral: int_{0}^{T/4} t^2 dt = \frac{(T/4)^3}{3} = \frac{T^3}{192}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Time-Domain Symmetric Triangular Waveform
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of displacement x(t) versus time t showing linear ramps rising from -A to +A at t = T/4 and falling from +A to -A at t = 3T/4.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the piecewise linear nature and temporal symmetry (odd function about t=0).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in identifying time period T, peak amplitude A, and slope changes.

solved_numericals.question: A symmetric triangular wave has a peak amplitude of 10 V. Calculate its RMS value.
solution_steps: Identify the peak amplitude: A = 10 V.
Apply the formula for the RMS value of a triangular wave: X_{rms} = A / sqrt(3).
Substitute values: X_{rms} = 10 / sqrt(3) approx 10 / 1.732 = 5.77 V.

solved_numericals.question: Find the ratio of the power contained in the third harmonic to that in the fundamental harmonic for a symmetric triangular wave.
solution_steps: Recall that the amplitude of the nth harmonic for a triangular wave varies as b_n propto 1/n².
The fundamental amplitude is b_1 and the third harmonic amplitude is b_3 = b_1 / 3² = b_1 / 9.
Power is proportional to the square of the amplitude: P_n propto b_n^2.
Calculate the power ratio: P_3 / P_1 = (b_3 / b_1)^2 = (1 / 9)^2 = 1 / 81.

solved_numericals.question: A triangular wave has a fundamental frequency of 50 Hz and a peak amplitude of 5 units. Write the expression for its second harmonic term.
solution_steps: Recall the Fourier series of a symmetric triangular wave contains only odd harmonics (n = 1, 3, 5, ...).
The coefficient for any even harmonic (such as n = 2) is zero due to half-wave and quarter-wave symmetries.
Therefore, the second harmonic term has an amplitude of zero.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes ideal piecewise linear segments with instantaneous slope reversals, which is physically unrealizable in real electronic circuits due to finite bandwidth limitations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Triangular waves contain both even and odd harmonics like general periodic signals.
common_misconceptions.correct: Symmetric triangular waves contain only odd harmonics.
common_misconceptions.why: The odd half-wave symmetry eliminates all even cosine and sine harmonic terms.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Harmonic amplitudes in a triangular wave decay as 1/n.
common_misconceptions.why: The 1/n decay rate belongs to square waves; continuous triangular waves have smoother corners leading to faster 1/n² attenuation.

quick_revision: Triangular wave Fourier series has only odd sine harmonics with 1/n² amplitude decay and RMS value equal to A / sqrt(3).
Fourier Series Expansion (Triangular Wave): x(t) = \frac{8A}{\pi^2} \sum_{n=1,3,5...}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{(n-1)/2}}{n^2} \sin(n\omega_0 t)
